title: RACHEL TRADED A NIGHT WITH HER HUSBAND FOR LEAH’S SON’S MANDRAKES—BUT WHAT GOD DID NEXT EXPOSES A HEARTBREAK MOST CHRISTIANS STILL HIDE
paragraphs: RACHEL TRADED A NIGHT WITH HER HUSBAND FOR LEAH’S SON’S MANDRAKES—BUT WHAT GOD DID NEXT EXPOSES A HEARTBREAK MOST CHRISTIANS STILL HIDE

Two sisters. One husband. A handful of mandrakes. And a desperate bargain in the middle of a broken family. Genesis 30:14–16 reveals something far deeper than jealousy and marital rivalry: the painful things people will trade when they are starving for love, desperate for significance, and struggling to trust God's timing. But behind this disturbing family scandal is a greater truth about the God who sees the forgotten, remembers the wounded, and ultimately brings redemption through Jesus Christ.
There are some stories in the Bible that make you want to close the book for a moment.
Not because they are difficult to understand.
But because they are painfully easy to recognize.
A woman who has her husband's affection but desperately wants a child.
Another woman who has given her husband children but desperately wants his affection.
Two sisters living under the same roof, measuring their worth against each other, silently bleeding from wounds neither knows how to heal.
And then comes a moment so strange, so uncomfortable, and so deeply human that you almost wonder why God allowed it to be recorded in Scripture.
Rachel traded a night with her own husband for some plants gathered by Leah's son.
Yes. That actually happened.
And before you judge either woman, consider this:
Have you ever been so desperate for something you did not have that you stopped recognizing the blessings already in your hands?
Have you ever watched someone else receive the very thing you had begged God for?
Have you ever smiled at somebody's blessing while secretly wondering why heaven seemed silent about yours?
Have you ever tried to negotiate your way into a miracle?
Because if you have, this ancient story is closer to your life than you might imagine.
And what happens after that night is something you cannot afford to miss.
The story begins long before the mandrakes.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Genesis 29 tells us that Jacob worked seven years to marry her, and those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
Imagine being loved like that.
Imagine someone willing to labor seven years just to build a future with you.
But on the wedding night, Jacob's father-in-law, Laban, deceived him.
Instead of Rachel, Laban gave him Leah.
By the time Jacob discovered what had happened, the marriage had already taken place.
Jacob eventually married Rachel as well, after fulfilling the bridal week with Leah, and committed himself to another seven years of service.
One man.
Two sisters.
One household already poisoned by deception, comparison, and unequal affection.
And here is the detail that should make us uncomfortable.
Leah had not orchestrated this arrangement according to the biblical account.
Yet she became the wife who lived with the knowledge that her husband loved her sister more.
Genesis 29:30 tells us that Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Think about what that meant.
Leah could share his home.
She could bear his children.
She could fulfill the expectations placed upon a wife in her culture.
But she could not force his heart to love her as he loved Rachel.
Some people know exactly what that feels like.
You are present, but not preferred.
Needed, but not cherished.
Useful, but somehow never enough.
You keep giving.
Keep serving.
Keep sacrificing.
And somewhere deep inside, a terrible question begins to grow.
What is wrong with me?
Then Scripture gives us one of the most tender and devastating statements in the entire account.
Genesis 29:31 says, in the King James Version:
“When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.”
The Hebrew text uses the word שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the root שָׂנֵא (sane'), meaning hated or unloved.

In this context, the surrounding verses establish that Leah was the less-loved wife. The wording communicates the painful disparity in Jacob's affection without requiring us to conclude that Jacob displayed active hostility toward her.
But notice something extraordinary.
The Lord saw Leah.
The Hebrew verb is וַיַּרְא (vayyar'), meaning “and he saw.”
Not merely that God possessed information about her circumstances.
The narrative draws our attention to the fact that her suffering was not hidden from Him.
Jacob saw Rachel with greater affection.
But God saw Leah in her humiliation.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
Being overlooked by people does not mean you are invisible to God.
The person who stopped appreciating you does not determine your value.
The relationship that failed to give you the love you needed does not determine your worth.
The family that constantly compares you with somebody else does not get the final word over your identity.
God saw Leah.
And He sees the person who has cried quietly because being strong in public became easier than admitting how deeply they were hurting.
But Leah's story becomes even more heartbreaking when we listen to the names she gives her children.
When Reuben is born, Leah says that the Lord has looked upon her affliction, and she hopes that now her husband will love her.
When Simeon is born, she recognizes that the Lord has heard that she is unloved.
When Levi is born, she hopes that her husband will finally become attached to her.
Can you hear the longing?
Maybe now he will love me.
Maybe this time he will notice me.
Maybe another child will make me enough.
Leah was receiving children, but she was still trying to obtain the affection she could not manufacture.
And then Judah was born.
Genesis 29:35 records her words:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
The Hebrew name יְהוּדָה (Yehudah) is associated in the passage with praise, from the Hebrew root ידה (y-d-h), which can express thanksgiving or praise.
For a moment, the focus of her words changes.
Not “Now my husband will love me.”
But “Now will I praise the LORD.”
That is a significant movement in the story.
Yet we must not pretend that Leah instantly became free from every insecurity.
Genesis 30 will show that her struggle continued.
And that is important.
Because spiritual growth is not always a straight line.
Sometimes you worship sincerely on Sunday and wrestle with the same old wound on Monday.
Sometimes you know God is faithful, yet still feel the sting of being overlooked.
Sometimes your lips praise Him while your heart is still learning to rest in Him.
God's work in us is not always completed in a single emotional moment.
Meanwhile, Rachel had her own suffering.
She was loved by Jacob.
But she could not conceive.
In the ancient world of Genesis, children were closely connected with family continuity, inheritance, and social standing. Infertility could carry tremendous personal grief and cultural shame.
Genesis 30:1 tells us that Rachel envied her sister and said to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Those are not the words of a woman who feels secure simply because she is loved.
Those are the words of a woman overwhelmed by longing.
Rachel had something Leah desperately wanted.
Leah had something Rachel desperately wanted.
And neither seemed able to enjoy what she possessed without being tormented by what she lacked.
Isn't that what comparison does?
It makes another person's blessing look like evidence of your own rejection.
It convinces you that if God gave something to somebody else, He must have forgotten you.
It turns gratitude into competition.
And before long, your prayer life becomes less about knowing God and more about keeping score.
Rachel's anguish was real.
Her longing for a child was not sinful in itself.
But envy was distorting her response to that longing.
Jacob became angry and answered:
“Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” (Genesis 30:2, KJV)
Jacob recognized that conception ultimately lay beyond his power.
But the exchange also reveals a household filled with pain and frustration.
Then Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob so that children might be born through her.
Leah later gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as well.
The family expanded.
But so did the rivalry.
The Bible records these arrangements without presenting their dysfunction as a model for Christian marriage.
This is a crucial distinction.
Not everything Scripture describes is something Scripture approves.
The broken decisions of the patriarchal family are not instructions for us to imitate.
They are part of the truthful record of human sin, suffering, and God's sovereign work amid deeply imperfect people.
Then, in the middle of the wheat harvest, something seemingly insignificant happened.
Leah's son Reuben went into the fields and found mandrakes.
Genesis 30:14 says:
“And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's mandrakes.”
The Hebrew word translated “mandrakes” is דּוּדָאִים (duda'im).
Mandrakes were plants associated in the ancient world with love and fertility. Their fragrant fruit and human-shaped roots contributed to various traditional beliefs about their properties.
But here is something we must understand clearly.
The Bible never says mandrakes have the power to cure infertility.
It does not teach believers to use them to conceive.
And it certainly does not say that Rachel eventually became pregnant because she obtained them.
Their significance in this narrative lies in what the women believed, desired, and were willing to exchange.
Rachel wanted the mandrakes.
Perhaps she hoped they might help her conceive, as their ancient reputation suggests.
The text does not explicitly explain her motive.
But it makes her desire unmistakable.
And Leah's response reveals that something far deeper than plants was at stake.
Genesis 30:15 records Leah saying:
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also?”
Read that again.
“Thou hast taken my husband.”
Leah was speaking to her own sister.
The woman who had been loved by Jacob from the beginning.
The woman Leah had spent years living beside, while carrying the wound of being less loved.
Her words were not merely about mandrakes.
They were about years of resentment.
Years of comparison.
Years of feeling displaced.
Years of asking whether she would ever truly belong.
And Rachel's response is almost unbelievable.
“Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.”
There it is.
The bargain.
A night with Jacob.
In exchange for Reuben's mandrakes.
The Hebrew expression יִשְׁכַּב עִמָּךְ הַלַּיְלָה (yishkav immakh hallaylah) means, in context, “he shall lie with you tonight.”
The verb שָׁכַב (shakhav) commonly means “to lie down,” and in passages like this it refers to sexual relations.
This was not a symbolic exchange.
The women were negotiating which wife would spend the night with Jacob.
And the text does not record Jacob participating in the negotiation.
That silence is part of what makes the account so unsettling.
A marriage relationship had become entangled in rivalry, bargaining, and competing desires.
Genesis 30:16 continues:

“And Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes. And he lay with her that night.”
Imagine the scene.
The sun is setting over the fields.
Jacob is returning from his work.
Leah walks out to meet him.
And instead of a tender invitation from a wife longing for her husband, the conversation becomes a declaration of an arrangement already made.
“I have hired thee.”
The Hebrew verb is from שָׂכַר (sakhar), meaning “to hire” or “to engage for wages.”
It is a painfully transactional expression.
A woman who had spent years longing to be loved now speaks of obtaining a night with her husband through a bargain.
And the woman who already possessed his greater affection had agreed to the exchange because she wanted something else.
What a picture of human brokenness.
Not because the women were uniquely wicked.
But because their suffering had become entangled with competition and attempts to control outcomes.
One woman wanted to be chosen.
The other wanted to become a mother.
And both were trying to secure what they could not ultimately guarantee.
Now here is where this ancient story walks straight into our modern lives.
We may not bargain with mandrakes.
But we know what it means to make desperate exchanges.
Some people trade their peace for approval.
Some trade their convictions for acceptance.
Some sacrifice their boundaries because they are terrified of being abandoned.
Some trade honesty for the appearance of a perfect family.
Some pursue relationships that compromise their faith because loneliness feels unbearable.
Some spend years trying to earn love from someone who has never learned to give it freely.
And some believers begin treating their relationship with God like a transaction.
“Lord, if I serve more, will You finally bless me?”
“If I give more, will You answer this prayer?”
“If I become a better Christian, will You remove this pain?”
“If I do everything right, will You give me the life I imagined?”
But God is not a merchant selling miracles.
And grace is not a commodity we purchase with religious performance.
There is a difference between trusting God in obedience and attempting to control Him through bargaining.
The Lord calls us to faithfulness.
He does not promise that every earthly desire will be fulfilled on our preferred schedule.
And that brings us to the next verse.
A verse many people rush past.
A verse that changes how we understand the entire episode.
Genesis 30:17 says:
“And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.”
Stop there.
It does not say the mandrakes made Leah conceive.
It says God listened to Leah.
The Hebrew reads:
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶל־לֵאָה
Vayyishma Elohim el-Le'ah.
“And God listened to Leah.”
The verb שָׁמַע (shama') means to hear or listen, and in many biblical contexts it carries the significance of responding attentively.
Scripture does not tell us the precise content of a prayer Leah may have offered at this moment.
We should not invent one.
But it does explicitly attribute her conception to God's attentive action.
Not to a plant.
Not to a bargain.
Not to a human formula.
To God.
Leah later gave birth to another son and eventually a daughter, Dinah, as the narrative continues.
And then comes the statement Rachel had been waiting for.
Genesis 30:22:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.”
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“And God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew verb זָכַר (zakhar) means “to remember.”
But when Scripture speaks of God remembering someone, it does not mean He previously forgot that person existed.
God is not absentminded.
In passages like this, divine remembrance signals God's purposeful attention and action.
He remembered Rachel.
He listened to her.
He opened her womb.
And Rachel conceived Joseph.
Notice the order.
Rachel obtained the mandrakes in Genesis 30:14–15.
Leah conceived in verse 17.
Rachel's conception is reported later, after Scripture explicitly says God remembered her.
The narrative never credits the mandrakes with producing Joseph.
It credits God.
And that distinction matters because human beings have always been tempted to place their confidence in something they can hold, purchase, arrange, or control.
A plant.
A ritual.
A formula.
A perfect strategy.
A religious performance.
Anything that promises certainty when faith feels frightening.
But Scripture keeps bringing us back to the Lord.
Not because every unanswered prayer is a punishment.
Not because every delay is a hidden test we can decode.
Not because faithful people are guaranteed marriage, children, healing, wealth, or earthly success.
But because our hope must ultimately rest in God's character rather than our ability to manufacture a desired outcome.
And we need to be careful here.
Rachel's eventual pregnancy is not a promise that every person struggling with infertility will conceive.
Leah's experience is not a promise that every neglected spouse will finally receive the affection they deserve.
These are historical events in God's unfolding redemptive plan, not universal guarantees of identical outcomes.
There are faithful Christians who pray for children and never have biological children.
There are believers who experience abandonment despite years of sincere love.
There are people who trust God deeply and still walk through grief that does not resolve the way they hoped.
Their suffering is not proof that God loves them less.
Their unanswered prayers are not proof that they failed to believe hard enough.
And their value in Christ is not measured by marriage, parenthood, fertility, popularity, or human approval.
That is why this story must not end with Joseph's birth.
Because if we stop there, we may miss the greatest redemption threaded through this deeply troubled family.
Look again at Leah.
The woman who was less loved.
The woman who spent years longing for her husband's affection.
The woman who cried out through the names of her children.
The woman who eventually named one son Judah and said, “Now will I praise the LORD.”
Judah's family line would become central to the unfolding story of redemption.
Genesis 49:10 associates Judah with royal authority.
Later, God's covenant with David develops the promise of a lasting royal house.
And in the New Testament, Matthew 1 traces the royal and messianic genealogy of Jesus Christ through Judah's line.
Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus:
“The Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David.”
Think about that.
The promised Messiah came through the line of Judah.
Judah was Leah's son.
The woman who was not Jacob's preferred wife became an ancestor in the royal line through which the Savior entered human history.
This does not mean Leah earned that privilege by suffering.
It does not mean her mistreatment was good.
And it does not mean God approved of the deception, rivalry, or marital disorder that marked the family.
It means God's redemptive purpose was not defeated by their brokenness.
Human rejection did not have the final word over Leah's place in God's unfolding story.
And there is another extraordinary truth here.
Joseph, Rachel's first son, would also become a central figure in Genesis.
His brothers would sell him into slavery.
He would suffer betrayal, false accusation, imprisonment, and years of separation.
Yet God would work through those events to preserve many lives.
Joseph would eventually tell his brothers in Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.”
Both sisters became part of a family history marked by profound sin and extraordinary divine providence.
But the Bible never asks us to admire the sin.
It asks us to recognize the God whose purposes cannot be overthrown by it.
And now we arrive at the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest problem in this story is not infertility.
It is not even the mandrake bargain.
It is the brokenness of human hearts living in a fallen world.
The longing to be loved.
The temptation to envy.
The desire to control.
The resentment that grows when comparison becomes a way of life.
The belief that possessing one more thing will finally make us whole.
Those struggles still live in us.
We may dress them in modern clothing.
We may hide them behind beautiful family photographs and carefully written social media captions.
We may sit in church, sing worship songs, and tell everybody we are fine.
But God knows where the heart is still wounded.
And He knows where woundedness has begun turning into sin.
Some of us need comfort.
Some of us need repentance.
Many of us need both.
Because pain can explain why we are struggling without justifying every decision we make because of that pain.
Leah's rejection was real.
Rachel's grief was real.
Their rivalry was real.
And their choices still had consequences.
The Gospel does not tell us to deny those realities.
It tells us that Jesus came to save sinners and reconcile us to God.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we solved every insecurity.
Not after we stopped making mistakes.
Not after we earned the right to be loved.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And this is where the story becomes intensely personal.
You may have spent years trying to prove that you are worthy of being chosen.
Perhaps you became the dependable one.
The successful one.
The beautiful one.
The strong one.
The person who never complains.
The Christian who never admits to struggling.
You learned to earn approval because receiving love without performing for it felt unfamiliar.
But Jesus does not invite you to purchase His mercy.
He calls you to repent and believe the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
A gift.
Not a wage.
Not a bargain.
Not a reward for becoming more lovable.
A gift of grace received through faith in Christ.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes genuine repentance possible without pretending that we can save ourselves.
You can confess the jealousy.
You can surrender the bitterness.
You can admit that you have been seeking identity in someone else's affection.
You can acknowledge that you have tried to manipulate circumstances because trusting God felt too vulnerable.
You can turn from sin and come to Jesus without first manufacturing a spotless history.
Because the cross declares that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
And grace is glorious enough that Christ willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Our hope is not that every painful circumstance will immediately change.
Our hope is that through His death and resurrection, Jesus offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life to all who believe in Him.
And the same Savior who forgives also begins transforming those who belong to Him.
He teaches us to stop measuring our worth by another person's attention.
To stop treating blessings as competitions.
To stop confusing control with faith.
To love without turning relationships into transactions.
To tell the truth about our wounds instead of allowing them to rule our decisions.
And to trust Him even when the outcome remains uncertain.
Maybe your mandrakes are not plants.
Maybe they are the approval you keep chasing.
The relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
The image you maintain because you are afraid people would reject the real you.
The comparison that quietly steals your joy every time you open Facebook.
The resentment you have nurtured for years because somebody else received what you wanted.
Or the desperate attempt to bargain with God for an answer He has not promised.
Whatever it is, ask yourself a difficult question.
What have I been willing to trade because I was afraid God would not be enough for me?
That question is not meant to shame you into silence.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
You do not have to disguise your desperation before Him.
You do not have to invent a spiritual explanation for every tear.
You do not have to pretend your faith has never trembled.
Come to Christ.
Bring the grief.
Bring the envy you are ashamed to admit.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the memories that still hurt.
Bring the sins you have been excusing.
Bring the parts of your life that look nothing like the testimony you hoped you would have.
And repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in His truth.
Because transformation begins not when we finally become capable of saving ourselves, but when we turn to the Savior who alone can redeem us.
And if this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Not to impress strangers.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
But because sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a conversation that helps another wounded believer stop pretending.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly. God already knows your story. But if you are willing, let your words open a door for prayer, encouragement, and genuine Christian fellowship.
Someone reading may need to know that following Jesus does not mean never struggling.
It means we do not have to struggle without hope.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish dramatic biblical stories.
Not merely to collect reactions or build another social media page.
But to keep directing people back to the Word of God, the finished work of Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the daily work of discipleship.
There are people scrolling through Facebook tonight who have not opened their Bible in months.
People who are spiritually hungry but do not know where to begin.
People who have mistaken religious activity for a living relationship with Christ.
People who are quietly drifting away.
And people who have never clearly understood the Gospel.
A faithful, Scripture-centered article cannot save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But God's Word can be faithfully proclaimed, and the Holy Spirit can use that truth to awaken conviction, encourage believers, and point people toward Christ.
That is why sharing this message matters.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because your friends and family may listen to a message that comes through someone they already know and trust.
Invite your family, Christian friends, struggling believers, and even those who are still exploring Christianity to follow as well.
The goal is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to help people encounter biblical truth and grow in their understanding of Jesus.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another way you can become part of its continued work.
For believers who are able and willing to give, this can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel-centered ministry.
But let us be biblically clear about something important.
It is not a spiritual requirement.
It does not replace your responsibility to support your local church or care for your household.
In Scripture, tithes and offerings have specific contexts, and the New Testament emphasizes willing, thoughtful, cheerful generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
These are simply tangible expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards.
Because discipleship is not a luxury reserved for people who can pay.
Because He is the One who deserves the glory.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return to that field one final time.
Picture Reuben carrying the mandrakes home.
Picture Rachel seeing something she hoped might give her what she lacked.
Picture Leah, still aching to be loved.
Picture Jacob walking back from the field, unaware of the bargain that had been made.
It was an ordinary evening in a profoundly troubled household.
No one there could have understood the full scope of what God would eventually do through this family.
Leah would become the mother of Judah.
Rachel would become the mother of Joseph.
Joseph would later help preserve the family through whom God's covenant promises would continue.
And generations later, from the tribe of Judah, Jesus Christ would come.
Not because the family was morally exemplary.
Not because their rivalry was holy.
Not because God needed their sin to accomplish His purpose.
But because God's covenant faithfulness was greater than their failures.
And this is where the title of our ministry becomes more than a phrase.
Not scandal excused.
Not sin celebrated.
Not suffering romanticized.
But real human brokenness met by the faithful purposes of a holy and merciful God.
And in Jesus Christ, grace does more than cover a shameful past.
It calls sinners to repentance.
It offers forgiveness.
It reconciles us to God.
It gives us a new identity.
And it begins rewriting the direction of a life that once seemed trapped by sin, fear, and shame.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not that every earthly consequence disappears.
It is that those who belong to Christ are made new in Him.
So if you have been living like Leah, trying to earn someone's love, remember that your ultimate worth is not determined by their preference.
If you have been living like Rachel, allowing an unfulfilled longing to consume your joy, remember that your identity is not defined by what you have not received.
If you have been comparing your life with somebody else's, repent of the envy and ask Christ to teach you gratitude and love.
If you have been bargaining with God, surrender the illusion that you can purchase His grace.
And if you have been running from Jesus because you are ashamed of your history, hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Come to Him.
Not with a transaction.
With repentance and faith.
Not with a perfect record.
With a genuine heart that knows it needs a Savior.
And if you do not yet know Christ, you can turn to Him today, confessing your sin, trusting in His death and resurrection, and calling upon Him for mercy.
You do not need a mandrake.
You do not need a bargain.
You need Jesus.
And if there is someone you love who is still trying to earn affection, outrun shame, or force a miracle, consider sharing this with them.
You may not know what God is doing in their heart.
But you can faithfully point them to the Savior.
And when you close this article, do not remember only the strange bargain between two sisters.
Remember the God who saw Leah.
The God who remembered Rachel.
The God who remained faithful to His covenant through a deeply imperfect family.
And above all, remember the Son of God who came into our broken world, bore our sins, rose victorious from the grave, and offers redemption to all who trust in Him.
You may have spent years trying to buy the love you were afraid you would never receive—but at the cross, Jesus offers a grace you could never afford and never have to purchase.
